concepts.name: Transformation Hierarchy of Computing
facts: Writing Y = Model(X) triggers a chain from algorithm design through program, system software, OS scheduling, and hardware execution, returning result Y to the application.

The workflow begins by designing an algorithm Model with input data X, then a program expresses that algorithm. System software turns the program into an executable, parallel, robust task, the OS schedules and deploys tasks onto hardware, and hardware executes instructions and moves data to produce Y.
Step 1: design an algorithm Model to solve a problem with input data X
Step 2: a program expresses the algorithm
Step 3: system software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task
Step 4: the OS schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware; hardware executes instructions and moves data
Step 5: computation completes and result Y is returned to the application
\( Y = \mathrm{Model}(X) \)

concepts.name: Instruction Execution and CPU Architecture Overview
facts: Instruction execution is the last step of computing, comprising load from RAM to register file, compute among registers, and store back to RAM, and its efficiency determines maximum computing power and speed.

A computing core has three components: ALU for computing, register file for data load/store, and instruction memory for pipelining. The Intel Xeon 6980P example shows 256 threads deciding parallelism, 3.2GHz deciding ALU/instruction execution speed, and 504MB cache deciding data load/store speed.
Load: from RAM to register file.
Compute: add, mul among registers.
Store: from register file to RAM.
Core components: ALU (computing), register file (load/store), instruction memory (pipelining).
CPU optimizes latency of a small number of complex threads.

concepts.name: Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline and Hazards
facts: The five-stage pipeline overlaps instruction execution across IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB stages to hide data load/store time, but hazards cause stalls and bubbles.

A perfect pipeline completes one instruction per cycle after filling, giving Total Cycles = M + N – 1 for N instructions and M stages. Any condition that stalls the pipeline is a hazard: data hazards arise from dependencies (RAW, WAW, WAR) and control hazards from branches, whose penalty worsens with deeper pipelines and whose uncertainty grows with branchy code.
Stages: Fetch (IF), Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), Write Back (WB)
Perfect pipeline: one instruction completes per cycle after filling, no bubbles
Data hazards: RAW, WAW, WAR dependencies
Control hazards: deeper pipeline causes worse penalty; branches create uncertainty
\( \text{Total Cycles} = M + N - 1 \)

concepts.name: Pipeline Optimizations: Data Forwarding and Register Renaming
facts: Data forwarding passes results directly from pipeline registers to ALU inputs so consumers execute earlier, while register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies.

Forwarding enables register-to-register or register-to-ALU paths, letting the consumer execute earlier and yielding fewer stalls and higher pipeline efficiency. Register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies, and the lecture illustrates both techniques with worked examples.

Consumer can execute earlier → fewer stalls, higher pipeline efficiency
Register renaming: more registers decouple dependencies

concepts.name: Advanced CPU Optimizations: OoO, Superscalar, Speculative Execution, Hyper-Threading
facts: OoO execution, superscalar issue, speculative execution with branch prediction, and hyper-threading each attack idle slots and stalls to raise latency and throughput.

OoO separates program order, execution order and commit order, with the compiler typically finding independent instruction sets to reduce stall time. Superscalar tries to execute multiple instructions per cycle via a wide pipeline (wide fetch/decode, multiple execution units, load/store paths, writeback, multi-ported register file), while speculative execution issues risky instructions for quick completion and a busy deep pipeline at the cost of wasted wrong-path work and recovery penalties; hyper-threading adds SMT so multiple hardware threads share one physical core.
OoO separates program order, execution order, and commit order
Superscalar needs a wide pipeline: wide fetch/decode, multiple execution units and load/store paths, wide writeback, multi-ported register file
Speculation benefit: low latency and high throughput; cost: wasted energy/cycles and recovery penalty growing with pipeline depth
Branch prediction: naïve static prediction lets the compiler remove not-taken branches; dynamic prediction also exists
Hyper-threading (SMT): multiple hardware threads share one physical core, each with its own architectural state

concepts.name: From CPU to GPU: Parallelism and Multiprocessors
facts: Throughput scaling moves beyond a single superscalar core by using many cores with a memory hierarchy, many servers with networking, and explicit parallelism.

A superscalar core reaches its ceiling through high frequency, deep pipeline and minimal hazards, so scaling means adding superscalar cores with memory hierarchy and servers with networking. Parallelism is data parallelism (vector and array processing) or task parallelism (multithreading); CPU scales to hundreds of heavy cores for control, GPU to 1,000s–10,000s of light cores for compute.
Single superscalar core ceiling: high frequency, deep pipeline, minimal hazards
Scale cores with memory hierarchy; scale servers with networking
Data parallelism: different pieces of data in parallel (vector/array processing)
Task parallelism: different tasks in parallel (multithreading)
CPU: control logic and dependencies cause synchronization, so hundreds of heavy cores; GPU: less control logic, easy data parallelism, so 1,000s–10,000s of light cores, 10x–100x CPU computing power

concepts.name: GPU Chip Organization and CUDA Programming Model
facts: A GPU chip has hundreds of streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each with processing units, a warp scheduler and shared memory, programmed via CUDA's kernel, thread block, warp and thread hierarchy.

Each SM contains simplified pipelines for specific precisions (INT32, FP32, FP64), a warp scheduler that packages threads into warps and switches to a ready warp when one waits, and high-speed shared memory for intra-SM exchange. A thread block is assigned to one SM (up to 8 blocks per SM; Fermi SM up to 1536 threads, e.g. 256*6 or 512*3 blocks), each block divided into 32-thread warps under SIMT, where threads in a warp should execute the same code but may take different branches.
CUDA hierarchy: kernel = GPU-level jobs, thread block = SM-level jobs, warp = minimal executing unit, thread = operator
SM units execute specific instructions for specific computing precision with simplified pipelines
Warp scheduler picks which warp runs per time slot; threads share a register file; when one warp waits, another ready warp is scheduled
Thread block assigned to one SM, up to 8 blocks per SM; Fermi SM up to 1536 threads
SIMT: threads in a warp should execute same instructions, but different branches are allowed

concepts.name: Control Divergence and SIMD Utilization
facts: Control divergence occurs when threads in a warp branch to different paths, so only a subset executes and SIMD pipeline utilization is wasted.

A GPU uses a SIMD pipeline to save area on control logic and groups scalar threads into warps; branch divergence arises when threads inside warps branch to different execution paths. Divergence-free programs increase SIMD utilization, and in vector reduction the optimized program keeps all active threads in the same warp.

Branch divergence: threads inside warps take different execution paths
Result: only a subset of threads execute, wasting SIMD utilization

concepts.name: CPU Multicore Programming with pThread
facts: pThread breaks a complex task into lightweight threads within one process that share the virtual address space, so global variables and heap objects are shared and synchronization is the programmer's job.

The pThread library (POSIX threads) is a standard for Unix-like systems linked with C/C++ programs; the example uses a fork-join pattern that partitions input into per-thread chunks for a parallel reduction. Because threads share memory, concurrent updates like sum += local_sum can race: each thread loads, adds and stores, so one write may overwrite another.
One process contains multiple threads sharing the same virtual address space.
Global variables and heap objects are shared across threads.
Synchronization is the programmer's responsibility.
pThread is a POSIX standard for Unix-like OSes, linked with C/C++ programs.

concepts.name: Synchronization Primitives: Mutex, Barriers, Condition Variables
facts: A mutex serializes access to a critical section so only one thread at a time updates protected shared state, while barriers and condition variables coordinate thread progress and waiting.

The mutex pattern wraps the critical section in pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock, giving race avoidance for protected shared state at the cost of lock contention, since other threads wait while one holds the lock. A barrier makes all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point, and a condition variable lets a thread sleep until a condition becomes true.
Mutex provides serialized access to the critical section and race avoidance for protected shared state.
Cost of a mutex is lock contention: only one thread holds it, others wait and the region is serialized.
Barrier: all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point; used in phase-based algorithms, debugging and iterative solvers.
Condition variable: a thread sleeps until a condition becomes true; used in worker pools and event-driven scheduling.

concepts.name: From pThread to CUDA: Same Idea, Different Granularity

pThread uses a few OS threads handling coarse tasks, while CUDA uses many logical threads each mapped to a data element, following the same SIMD/SIMT pattern. The work unit and launch API differ: pthread_create/pthread_join versus CUDA thread/data element and kernel launch.

CUDA: many logical threads, data elements
Same SIMD/SIMT pattern underlies both models

concepts.name: Amdahl's Law

study_notes.title: Advanced CPU Optimizations: OoO, Superscalar, Speculative Execution, Hyper-Threading

required_points.text: OoO execution, superscalar issue, speculative execution with branch prediction, and hyper-threading each attack idle slots and stalls to raise latency and throughput.

evidence.quote:
CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads
  Optimization #3: Out-of-Order (OoO) Execution
¡  Out-of-order execution separates:

   ¡ Program order: order written by the programmer

   ¡  Execution order: order chosen by hardware
   ¡ Commit order: order that updates architectural state


¡  Typically, the compiler would find independent instruction sets to enable OoO execution, reducing
   the stall time of the instruction pipeline.

¡ At runtime, CPU involves a controller to find independent instructions while some instructions are
   waiting.

   ¡  Preempt current pipeline

   ¡  Issue independent instruction

   ¡  Restore preempted instruction when it finishes waiting

required_points.text: OoO separates program order, execution order and commit order, with the compiler typically finding independent instruction sets to reduce stall time. Superscalar tries to execute multiple instructions per cycle via a wide pipeline (wide fetch/decode, multiple execution units, load/store paths, writeback, multi-ported register file), while speculative execution issues risky instructions for quick completion and a busy deep pipeline at the cost of wasted wrong-path work and recovery penalties; hyper-threading adds SMT so multiple hardware threads share one physical core.

study_notes.title: GPU Chip Organization and CUDA Programming Model

required_points.text: A GPU chip has hundreds of streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each with processing units, a warp scheduler and shared memory, programmed via CUDA's kernel, thread block, warp and thread hierarchy.

evidence.quote:

    Chip Organization

¡  Hundreds of Streaming Multiprocessors
   (SM)s


¡  Each SM consists of:
   ¡   Processing units, e.g., INT32, FP32, FP64, etc.
       ¡   Simplified pipelines compared to CPU cores.
       ¡  Each unit executes specific instructions that are
            designed to specific computing precision.
   ¡  Warp Scheduler
       ¡  When deploy multiple threads, GPU packages a
           branch of threads into a warp.
       ¡  The scheduler decides which warp would run at one
           time slot, and these threads shard a register file.
       ¡  When one warp waits, schedule another ready warp.
   ¡  High-speed shared memory for intra-SM data
       exchange.
   ¡  Tensor core: accelerator for matrix operations.

required_points.text: Each SM contains simplified pipelines for specific precisions (INT32, FP32, FP64), a warp scheduler that packages threads into warps and switches to a ready warp when one waits, and high-speed shared memory for intra-SM exchange. A thread block is assigned to one SM (up to 8 blocks per SM; Fermi SM up to 1536 threads, e.g. 256*6 or 512*3 blocks), each block divided into 32-thread warps under SIMT, where threads in a warp should execute the same code but may take different branches.

study_notes.title: Synchronization Primitives: Mutex, Barriers, Condition Variables

required_points.text: A mutex serializes access to a critical section so only one thread at a time updates protected shared state, while barriers and condition variables coordinate thread progress and waiting.

The mutex pattern wraps the critical section in pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock, giving race avoidance for protected shared state at the cost of lock contention, since other threads wait while one holds the lock. A barrier makes all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point, and a condition variable lets a thread sleep until a condition becomes true.
Mutex provides serialized access to the critical section and race avoidance for protected shared state.
Cost of a mutex is lock contention: only one thread holds it, others wait and the region is serialized.
Barrier: all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point; used in phase-based algorithms, debugging and iterative solvers.
Condition variable: a thread sleeps until a condition becomes true; used in worker pools and event-driven scheduling.

study_notes.title: CUDA Program Structure, Kernel Definition, and Synchronization

required_points.text: CUDA starts on the CPU: host code allocates device memory, copies data, launches the kernel asynchronously, and copies results back.

evidence.quote:
GPU Programming: CUDA
  CUDA Program Structure


¡ CUDA starts on the CPU: host code manages device memory, data movement, and kernel launch.





   Host memory        copy     Device memory       launch    Kernel execution      copy      Host result
      h_A, h_B, h_C                    d_A, d_B, d_C                   vecAdd<<<...>>>                   h_C





     cudaMalloc(&d_A, bytes);                                                 Important detail
     cudaMemcpy(d_A, h_A, bytes, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);                            Kernel launch is asynchronous.
     vecAdd<<<numBlocks, blockSize>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, n);
                                                                                 Use cudaDeviceSynchronize() or a     cudaMemcpy(h_C, d_C, bytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);
                                                                                                     blocking copy/event when host
     cudaFree(d_A);                                                                                     code needs the result.

required_points.text: The host uses cudaMalloc and cudaMemcpy to move h_A/h_B to d_A/d_B, launches vecAdd<<<numBlocks, blockSize>>>, then copies d_C back to h_C. Because kernel launch is asynchronous, cudaDeviceSynchronize() or a blocking copy is needed.

                                                          FIXED PROBLEM SIZE

1 - f: serial fraction

NUMERICAL INTUITION

             f = 0.90                                 f = 0.99

    max speedup -> 10x          max speedup -> 100x

required_points.text: With parallelizable fraction f and serial fraction 1-f, adding processors reduces the parallel term f/p but the serial part remains. Numerically, f=0.90 caps speedup near 10x and f=0.99 near 100x.
